property_summary: Only the contract owner can successfully call withdrawAll (so calling withdrawAll from a non-owner must revert).
Calls to withdrawAll must revert when invoked by the contract owner (msg.sender == owner).
When the test caller is the owner, calling withdrawAll should revert.
When the test caller is the recorded owner of c, calling withdrawAll should revert.
When this test caller meets the precondition, calling c.withdrawAll() must revert (i.e., reverted == true).

For any caller and any sendMoney arguments, only the contract deployer (owner) can later withdraw all funds via withdrawAll; the mutant inverts onlyOwner allowing non-owners to withdraw, so there exist inputs where a non-owner can withdraw and thus the property is violated.

For any nonzero balance funded to the contract and when the owner calls withdrawAll(), the reference contract always transfers the contract's full balance to the owner (leaving address(c).balance == 0), whereas the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a nonzero balance; the test fuzzes an initial deposit amount so the mutant fails for some inputs.

For any nonzero Ether deposited into C, calling withdrawAll by the owner always sets address(c).balance == 0 (reference); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a nonzero balance and thus violates this property for some deposit amounts.

If the contract has a positive balance and the owner calls withdrawAll, the reference transfers that entire balance out (leaving address(c).balance == 0); the mutant calling withdraw(0) can leave a nonzero balance, so the property 'after owner calls withdrawAll the contract balance is zero' holds for the reference for all admissible inputs but is violated by the mutant for some inputs.

If the owner calls withdrawAll immediately after sending a nonzero amount to the contract via a low-level call that executes fallback (i.e., the contract has positive balance and the owner calls withdrawAll), then the reference sends that entire balance to the owner (so address(c).balance == 0 after withdrawAll); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave the balance nonzero — we detect this by having an adversarial depositor perform the deposit via a helper contract that calls the target with value, then the owner calls withdrawAll and we assert the contract balance is zero (the reference satisfies this for all admissible inputs; the mutant fails for some).

For any nonzero deposit amount and any depositor, if the owner calls withdrawAll then the contract's balance becomes equal to the contract balance minus the amount transferred to the owner (i.e., the owner receives all available balance so address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can violate this by leaving a positive contract balance after withdrawAll.

Reference contract C ensures only the owner can withdraw the entire contract balance via withdrawAll() for every caller; the mutant removes onlyOwner so some non-owner caller can make address(c).balance become zero, violating that property.

For all callers, calling withdrawAll() does not change the contract balance unless the caller is the owner; the reference enforces onlyOwner so non-owners cannot drain the contract, whereas the mutant (removed onlyOwner) allows some non-owner caller to reduce address(c).balance to 0.

For every caller, calling withdrawAll() either reverts (if caller is not owner) or succeeds and sets address(c).balance to 0 (if caller is owner); the mutant removes the owner check so some non-owner caller can successfully drain the contract and make address(c).balance == 0, which violates the rule that only the owner can make the contract balance zero via withdrawAll().

For every caller, calling withdrawAll() on C either reverts (if caller is not the owner) or (if caller is the owner) succeeds and transfers the contract balance out; the mutant removes the onlyOwner check so some non-owner caller can successfully call withdrawAll() and drain the contract — violating that non-owners cannot successfully invoke withdrawAll().

For every caller address, calling withdrawAll() either reverts (if the caller is not owner) or succeeds (if owner); therefore any non-owner caller cannot successfully drain the contract balance via withdrawAll(), but the mutant (removed onlyOwner) allows some non-owner caller to successfully call withdrawAll() — violating this rule.

Reference contract always sends all contract balance to the owner when withdrawAll() is called (owner receives balance and contract balance becomes zero); the mutant uses sendMoney which performs a low-level call to an external address and can fail or behave differently (e.g., revert/consume gas/forward different gas) causing the owner not to receive funds and contract balance to remain non-zero for some inputs (adversarial callee).

For any caller that is the owner and any ether balance in the contract, calling withdrawAll() always empties the contract balance (leaving address(c).balance == 0); the mutant replaces transfer with a low-level call to the recipient which can fail/consume gas and therefore can leave non-zero contract balance for some adversarial callee address.

For any owner who calls withdrawAll when the contract holds any ETH, the reference implementation always empties the contract (address(c).balance == 0) because transfer to the owner cannot fail, whereas the mutant uses a low-level call to the recipient which can fail (e.g., if the recipient reverts on receive), leaving a non-zero contract balance for some adversarial recipient.

For any owner caller and any contract balance, calling withdrawAll() on the correct contract always results in the contract balance becoming zero (funds are transferred to the owner); the mutant uses a low-level call to an external target, so when that target's fallback reverts the call can fail and the contract balance can remain non-zero for some inputs.

For any owner and any nonzero contract balance, calling withdrawAll() always results in the contract's balance becoming zero on the correct contract; the mutant that calls an external target via low-level call can fail when the recipient reverts, leaving a nonzero contract balance for some adversarial recipient address.

For any withdrawn amount and owner caller, the reference contract always reduces contract balance by the withdrawn amount (withdraw transfers succeed or revert), whereas the mutant using send may silently fail leaving the contract balance unchanged for some inputs (failing callee), so address(c).balance == initialBalance - amount always holds for the reference but can fail for the mutant.

For any caller and any withdrawal amount performed by the owner to a callee that may revert, the reference contract always makes the contract balance decrease by the requested amount (it either succeeds or reverts), whereas the mutant that uses send can silently fail when the callee reverts, leaving address(c).balance unchanged and thus violating the balance-decrease rule for some inputs.

For any caller and any amount, calling withdraw(amount) by the owner always transfers that amount out of the contract (reducing address(c).balance by that amount); the mutant uses call(...) and ignores failure, so when the recipient reverts the transfer the reference still reverts (preventing the call) but the mutant will silently keep the funds, violating the rule for some inputs (a reverting recipient).

For any recipient and amount, when the contract owner calls withdraw(amount) the reference implementation always transfers the requested amount out (so address(c).balance decreases by amount) whereas the mutant that replaces transfer with a low-level call can fail to transfer to a reverting recipient and thus keep the funds for some inputs (a recipient that reverts).

For every target recipient address that reverts on receiving Ether, the correct contract's withdraw(...) call (using transfer) will revert (so address(c).balance does not decrease), whereas the mutant using low-level call will not revert and may keep the funds; thus the property: when withdrawing to a reverting recipient, the call to withdraw must revert (ok == false), which holds for the reference and is violated by the mutant for some inputs.

Reference C enforces that only the externally owned owner address can cause ETH to be withdrawn (calls to withdraw from any other EOA or contract address must not succeed in changing contract balance), whereas the mutant wrongly allows the contract itself to call withdraw and so a re-entrant/contract-invoked withdraw can siphon funds; the property: after any call to withdraw initiated by any external account depositing funds and then invoking withdraw, the contract balance is zero only when the caller is the owner — reference preserves that invariant for all inputs, mutant can violate it for some input where the contract itself (via a helper) triggers withdraw.

For any caller and any amount, only an external owner EOA can successfully cause the contract to transfer out ETH via withdraw; the mutant that also allows the contract itself to call withdraw enables a contract-based caller to withdraw funds (violating the rule) for some inputs.

For every caller and amount, only the externally-owned owner address (msg.sender == owner) can successfully cause the contract to transfer out ETH via withdraw; the mutant that also allows the contract itself (msg.sender == address(this)) to be treated as owner lets an internal contract call path drain funds for some inputs, violating this rule.

Invariant: For every caller address and amount, if a non-owner externally-owned account (EOA) calls withdraw after funding the contract, the call must revert (i.e., only the owner EOA can successfully invoke withdraw); the mutant that relaxes onlyOwner to allow address(this) may let an internal contract invocation succeed for some fuzzed inputs, violating this rule.

For every caller and deposit amount, if withdraw is invoked directly by an EOA (not the contract itself) then only the original owner can successfully make the contract send funds (reference: withdraw succeeds only when msg.sender == owner); the mutant that allows msg.sender == address(this) can succeed when a contract triggers withdraw, so there exists a contract-caller input that the mutant accepts but the reference rejects.

After attempting to send ETH via sendMoney, the target's call failure does not revert and therefore c's balance may decrease while depositsCount stays unchanged (i.e., sendMoney never reverts on target failure), so calling sendMoney cannot always be observed to revert; specifically, for any amount <= address(c).balance, sendMoney either succeeds (no revert) or, if target consumes no gas and reverts, original P still does not revert but loses balance — thus assert that sendMoney does not always revert (we check that a call attempt returns success or c balance decreased).
